Listening · Exercises 2–3

Keeping in touch

Listen to Recording 2. First decide True or False, then choose a, b or c.

Show transcript
Presenter: Thanks for joining us, Ruth. Maybe you could begin by telling us what you did after you left school. Ruth: After school, I moved to Peru. I applied to be an assistant on a research trip exploring ancient ruins near Cusco. I loved it and decided to stay in Peru and raise money for the project. I lived there for five years and lost contact with everyone in the UK because my work was usually in places with no phone signal or internet. I finished my work there, toured South America, then ran out of money and came back to Scotland to find a job. It took a long time to catch up with old friends because some had moved to different cities for university and work. Luckily, my best friend Sue didn’t move away. We’ve been visiting art galleries and museums. A couple of months ago we took up tennis. Sue beats me every time! I’ve just started a new job. The researcher who led the Cusco trip suggested that we set up a charity in Glasgow to raise money for the project in Peru. Next month I’m going to the US to meet people interested in our project. I don’t think Sue will miss me too much: she’s going out with Darren, who works for a film company based here in Glasgow. We’ve discussed him producing a film for our charity.

Reading · Exercises 11–12

A move to Indonesia

The Anderson family

People say that moving house is one of the most stressful things you can do, but the Anderson family moved continents: 7,000 miles from England to Indonesia.

Jenny Anderson loves animals and was studying for a PhD in Animal Conservation. She contacted an organisation in Sumatra to ask questions about orangutans for her research. They offered her a job. Her husband Len enjoyed his engineering job, and they had two young children, Keira and Ben, so Jenny had to think carefully. Len saw it as a fantastic opportunity and agreed to move.

Indonesia was much hotter than the UK, and the rain was extremely heavy. Their street flooded, so they sometimes walked through knee-deep water. Their house had no hot water or shower; they washed with cold water from a bucket. At first they wondered if leaving England had been a mistake. The roads were more crowded, the food was spicier and everywhere was louder.

After a couple of weeks, they began to enjoy the differences. They found Indonesian people very friendly. Jenny loved her job, and the children grew up near the rainforest, seeing orangutans, elephants and monkeys. They sent animal photos to their friends back home. They are not planning to move back to England yet, although they enjoy visiting.
